new_entities.name: Long working hours
new_entities.description: Occupational exposure to persistently long work schedules or high overtime hours.

edges.effect_quant: The overall hypertension signal for long work hours is inconsistent: pooled data are near-null overall, though some subgroup analyses, especially in women, point upward.
edges.population: working adults exposed to extended work hours or overtime
edges.mechanism: Long work hours can worsen stress physiology, sleep, and recovery time in ways that plausibly raise blood pressure. At the same time, healthy-worker selection and occupation-specific differences can distort cross-sectional findings and even reverse the observed association.
edges.summary: This edge is a good example of why not every plausible occupational risk gets a clean directional label. The newest meta-analysis was near-null overall for hypertension, an umbrella review rated the broader evidence as unclear, and one large Japanese overtime study even found an inverse cross-sectional association.
edges.caveats: Cross-sectional designs and healthy-worker bias matter a lot here, because workers able to sustain the longest hours may differ systematically from those who cannot. The safest framing is mixed evidence with possible subgroup risk rather than a settled harmful effect.

evidence.citation: Song JH et al 2024 J Epidemiol Community Health
evidence.notes: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the association between long working hours and hypertension risk.

effect_quant.comparator: long working hours versus non-long working hours for hypertension

evidence.notes: Shift work and long work hours and their association with chronic health conditions: A systematic review of systematic reviews with meta-analyses.
